cards.front: Recall a key point about Working with Watercolour and Acrylic
cards.back: Watercolour relies on the white of the paper for luminosity — work from light to dark, preserving highlights.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Working with Watercolour and Acrylic
cards.back: Acrylic is versatile: thin it for washes or apply thickly (impasto) for texture; it dries quickly so you can layer rapidly.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Working with Watercolour and Acrylic
cards.back: Wash techniques include flat wash (even tone), graded wash (light to dark), and wet-on-wet (blended, soft edges).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Working with Watercolour and Acrylic
cards.back: Glazing (thin transparent layers over dried paint) builds depth and richness in both watercolour and acrylic.

cards.front: What should you know about fine art exam tips?
cards.back: Show PROCESS, not just outcome — include test strips, colour wheels, wash experiments. Annotate with technique names and explanations. Compare the same subject rendered in different paint media.

Students often make mistakes with this topic. Wrong: Keep adding paint and scrubbing to get darker tones in watercolour. Correct: Watercolour's beauty is its transparency — build tone with thin GLAZES, not thick layers. Overworking creates muddy, dull areas. Plan highlights in advance — you cannot easily restore them once lost.
Create a series of paint experiments showing at least four different watercolour or acrylic techniques. Annotate each sample explaining the process, its effect and when you might use it.

cards.front: Assessment Objective Focus: Working with Watercolour and Acrylic
cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Demonstrate knowledge of Working with Watercolour and Acrylic using appropriate art vocabulary. Identify techniques, materials and processes accurately.
